title: Traffic — how many people viewed your site, and how many contacted you
body:
On the **„Traffic”** tab you get the answer to one question: **was it worth it?** We do not show tables,
just a single sentence about how many guests viewed your site and how many of them
contacted you.

![Screenshot: the Traffic tab on a phone](assets/hu/screen.png)

## What do the numbers mean?

- **Guests** — how many separate visitors opened your site. ⚠️ **We count per day:** someone who
  looks again several times within one day counts once — but someone who comes back on another day
  is counted as a new guest. This is because **we do not track your
  visitors across days**: the identifier used to tell them apart is destroyed every night,
  so no profile can be built from it. In other words, the number is cautious rather than flattering.
- **Views** — how many times the site was opened in total. This is always more than (or equal to)
  the number of guests.
- **Contacts (bookings, inquiries)** — how many people sent you a booking request or a message
  from the site. **This is what matters**: these are the real guests.
- **Came from Google** — what percentage of views came from the Google search engine
  (from any Google address: google.hu, google.com and the rest).
- **Viewed on a phone** — what percentage of views happened on a mobile or tablet.
  (Usually the majority — which is also why it matters that your site looks good on a phone.)

## “Every 20th visitor becomes a contact”

Below the numbers, this sentence shows the share of browsing that turns into real
interest. This is the most telling figure: if the ratio improves, your site is working harder.

⚠️ This sentence only appears once **there has been at least one contact** — without one
there would be nothing to compare.

## If you have your own web address

If you ordered your own domain, a separate sentence shows how many views arrived at **your own
address** and how many at the citoviso address. From this you can see how well the new address has caught on.

Without your own web address, this sentence simply does not appear.

## Period

You can choose between two buttons: **„Last 30 days”** (the default) and **„Last 7 days”**. Switching
recalculates the whole screen.

## “Nothing to show yet”

If your site went live recently, you see this message. It is **not an error**: simply nobody has
opened it yet. As soon as the first guest arrives, the numbers appear by themselves.

We deliberately do not show a table full of zeros — it would tell you nothing.

## Why don't the numbers match other analytics tools?

Two kinds of difference occur, and both are intentional:

- **We do not count search engine robots.** Google and the other search engines read through your site
  several times a day — these are machines, not guests. If we counted them, we would show a nicer but false
  number.
- **We do not measure with cookies.** We measure on our own server, so you do not need to
  display a cookie notice, and we do not build profiles of your visitors. Visitors
  are told apart with an identifier that restarts every day and cannot be reversed.

## Do you get an email about it?

Yes. **Once a month** we also send you the same numbers by email (for the past 30 days),
so you do not have to log in for them. The exact period is in the email's subject and first line
(for example “14 September – 14 October”). The email contains a button that opens
this screen in one click.

You get the **first email once your site has been live for at least 3 weeks** — before that, for most of the 30-day
period the site did not even exist yet, so the numbers would tell you nothing.

⚠️ **We do not send an email for a month in which nobody opened your site.** A
“0 guests” email would tell you nothing — in that case we would rather stay quiet.
